## Secret Mystery ADT

First, speculate on what type of data you can put into it!

\

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
<u>YES&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;</u>
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
<u>NO&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;</u>
:::
::::

::: notes
The bag. Students call out types; you say yes or no.

YES: anything with comparable keys: ints, strings, dates, (priority, job)
pairs, students ordered by student number.

NO: things with no natural order: colours, sets, images, a `struct`
without an `operator<`.

The rule they're meant to infer: you have to be able to compare two keys.
:::

## Secret Mystery ADT

\
\
\
\
\

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
ADT: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

insert

remove

getSize
:::
::::

::: notes
Students name items to insert; draw them in the bag.

Then ask for a remove. They want to say which one: they can't. You tell
them what comes out, the smallest key, each time.

ADT: **priority queue**. `insert`, `removeMin`, `getSize`.
:::

::: notes
Fill in each row's insert and removeMin.

- Unsorted array: insert $O(1)$ (amortized: $O(n)$ when it has to grow),
  removeMin $O(n)$ to find the min and fill the hole.
- Unsorted list: insert $O(1)$ at the front, removeMin $O(n)$.
- Sorted array: insert $O(n)$ (binary search finds the spot in $O(\log n)$,
  but the shift is $O(n)$), removeMin $O(1)$ if it's sorted largest-first,
  so the min is at the end.
- Sorted list: insert $O(n)$ (no binary search on a list), removeMin $O(1)$
  from the front.

Every option is $O(n)$ somewhere. Can we get both down to $O(\log n)$?
:::

Describe its implementation...

::: notes
- Binary tree, **complete**: every level full except possibly the last,
  which fills left to right.
- **Heap property** (min-heap): every node's key is $\le$ its children's.
  So the min is at the root.
- No left/right order between siblings: this is not a BST.
- Height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, because it's complete.

Implementation: the colours are a hint. Complete means no gaps, so read it
level by level into an array.
:::

::: notes
Root at index 1 (index 0 left empty).

For the node at index $i$:

- left child $2i$
- right child $2i + 1$
- parent $\lfloor i/2 \rfloor$

No pointers at all: the shape is the arithmetic.
:::

::: notes
The box is `size`; the three empty cells are spare capacity.

Try insert(5): it goes in the next free slot, index 13 (right child of 7).
Then swap upward while it's smaller than its parent: past 7, past 6, and it
stops under 4. Repeat with insert(3) to reach the root.

$O(\log n)$: at most one swap per level.
:::

}

::: notes
When the array is full: double the capacity and copy. The new last level
needs as many slots as the whole tree so far. Doubling makes insert
amortized $O(1)$ for the growing, plus $O(\log n)$ for heapifyUp.
:::

## Code: {.smaller .midcode}

```cpp
void heap<T>::insert(const T & key) {
    if (size == capacity) growArray();
    size++;
    items[size] = key;
    heapifyUp(size);
}
```

```cpp
void heap<T>::heapifyUp(int cIndex) {
    if (cIndex > _____)
        if (items[cIndex] ___ items[parent(cIndex)]) {
            swap(__________, __________);
            heapifyUp(__________);
        }
}
```

::: notes
- `cIndex > 1`: stop at the root
- `items[cIndex] < items[parent(cIndex)]`
- `swap(items[cIndex], items[parent(cIndex)])`
- `heapifyUp(parent(cIndex))`
:::

::: notes
The min is the root. What fills the hole and keeps the tree complete? Only
the last leaf can move without leaving a gap: 11 goes to the root.

Then swap it downward with its **smaller** child while it's bigger: 11
swaps with 5, then with 9, and stops: its new children, 14 and 12, are
both bigger.

$O(\log n)$.
:::

## Code: {.smaller .midcode}

```cpp
T heap<T>::removeMin() {
    T minVal = items[1];
    items[1] = items[size];
    size--;
    heapifyDown(1);
    return minVal;
}
```

```cpp
void heap<T>::heapifyDown(int cIndex) {
    if (hasAChild(cIndex)) {
        minChildIndex = minChild(cIndex);
        if (items[cIndex] ___ items[minChildIndex]) {
            swap(__________, __________);
            ___________________________
        }
    }
}
```

::: notes
- `items[cIndex] > items[minChildIndex]`
- `swap(items[cIndex], items[minChildIndex])`
- `heapifyDown(minChildIndex);`

Why the min child? Swapping with the larger one would put it above the
smaller one, breaking the heap property right there.
:::
